stops.name: Vado del Yeso, the annihilation of Joaquín and the death of Tania
stops.campa: A peasant named Honorato Rojas, bought by the army, leads Joaquín's lost rearguard to a ford on the Masicuri where Captain Vargas's soldiers wait in the reeds. As the column wades the Río Grande at dusk, guns high, the volley comes: Joaquín, the veterans, and Tania the guerrillera die in the water, her body carried downstream for days. Che, marching to find them, hears the news on the enemy's radio and refuses it as psychological warfare, until the details harden into fact. The rearguard is erased entire. The diary's September opens with seventeen men left, and the noose visible.

stops.name: Alto Seco, the last sermon
stops.campa: The seventeen climb out of the canyons into the cold hamlet of Alto Seco, fifty mud houses at nineteen hundred meters, and buy food from wary villagers whose mayor has already slipped away to inform. That evening, in the little schoolhouse by lamplight, Inti speaks to the assembled peasants about the revolution while Che, gaunt, watches and adds his words; the audience listens in silence and asks about bread. It is the guerrilla's last address to the people it came for: a sermon in an empty church, recorded in the diary with dry, unsparing affection.
stops.quote: Alto Seco is a little village of fifty houses, situated at 1,900 meters altitude, which received us with a well-orchestrated mixture of fear and curiosity.
stops.quote_source: Che Guevara, The Bolivian Diary, 22 September 1967

stops.name: La Higuera trail, the ambush of 26 September, 'Defeat'
stops.campa: Descending toward the village of La Higuera, the vanguard walks into an army ambush on the trail from Picacho. Coco Peredo, the guerrilla's Bolivian heart, is killed with Miguel and Julio; the column scatters into the gullies under fire, and deserters begin naming names to the Rangers. That night Che opens the diary entry with a single word: Defeat, written the way he writes everything, as fact to be used. The ring of soldiers around the Vallegrande canyons draws tight. Twelve days of life remain, and the diary does not change its tone by one degree.
stops.quote_source: Che Guevara, The Bolivian Diary, 26 September 1967, first word of the entry

stops.name: Quebrada del Yuro, the last battle and the capture
stops.campa: Betrayed by a peasant who saw them enter the ravine, the last seventeen are pinned in the Quebrada del Yuro at midday by the new Ranger battalion. Che fights until a bullet destroys his carbine and another tears his leg; hauled up wounded between two comrades, he is cornered by soldiers whose sergeant nearly fires. The prisoner speaks the sentence the trial-record of the canon preserves: he names himself, and appraises his own worth alive. The night before, his final diary entry had recorded, almost gently, that the eleven-month anniversary passed in a bucolic mood. The diary ends; the Passion begins.
stops.quote: Don't shoot! I am Che Guevara, and I am worth more to you alive than dead.
stops.quote_source: Words at capture, Quebrada del Yuro, 8 October 1967, as recorded in Bolivian soldiers' testimony and the canonical accounts

stops.name: La Higuera, the schoolhouse, 9 October 1967
stops.campa: He lies bound all night on the mud floor of the village schoolhouse beside the bodies of his comrades. To the schoolteacher Julia Cortez, who brings him soup, he observes that in Bolivia teachers earn less than the officials' cars are worth, and that the school's walls need paint. At midday the order comes down from the government by radio: no trial. Sergeant Mario Terán enters with his rifle and hesitates before the calm of the prisoner, who speaks to him the sentence with which the canon closes the life, steadying his own executioner's aim. The burst comes. It is one in the afternoon.
stops.quote: Ponte sereno y apunta bien. Vas a matar a un hombre. — Calm yourself, and aim well. You are going to kill a man.
stops.quote_source: Last words to Mario Terán in the La Higuera schoolhouse, 9 October 1967, as fixed in the canonical accounts

stops.name: Vallegrande, the laundry house of Nuestra Señora de Malta
stops.campa: Lashed to the skid of a helicopter, the body is flown to Vallegrande and laid on the concrete washbasin of the hospital laundry, shirtless, eyes open. For two days the town files past; nuns and washerwomen murmur that he looks like Christ taken down, and snip locks of his hair for relics. Freddy Alborta's photograph fixes the scene forever: the officers pointing like donors in an old master. The hands are cut off for the fingerprint archive; the body vanishes into a secret pit by the airstrip, to sleep thirty years until Cuba brings the bones home to a mausoleum at Santa Clara, city of the armored train.
